title: Exact pipeline stage where customers drop off
question: At which stage do deals stop, when they end without a win?
how_to_read: Each bar is the stage the deal sat in when it was marked lost or abandoned. Abandoned means nobody ever marked it lost — a follow-up failure, not a sales loss.

footer.learns: 48 of the 142 deals that closed without a win stopped at Waiting On Details, and 35 of those were never marked lost at all.
footer.does: Take the top bar and ask what has to change at that stage. High abandoned share at a stage is a process problem, not a pricing problem.

blocks.subtitle: Stage the deal was in when it closed
Share lost against abandoned, by stage

title: Conversion rate between every stage and the next
question: What share of deals that reach a stage go on to the next one?
how_to_read: Each step is deals whose furthest stage is this one or later. The percentage is how many carried on.

footer.learns: Deals hold up to the quote — 91% to 97% carry on at each early stage — then 302 at Quote Sent become 72 at Negotiation.
footer.does: The biggest single drop is the cheapest thing to fix.

title: Why deals were lost
question: On deals that ended without a win, was a reason written down?
caveat: Reason recorded on a minority of deals. Omnia has none at all.
how_to_read: The grey portion is deals where nobody wrote a reason. Themes come from keyword matching on meddic_9, the only field where a real reason is written.

footer.learns: Only 19 of the 142 closed-without-win deals carry a written reason. Of those, price, below minimum order and no response tie on 5 each.
footer.does: Until the grey shrinks, the themes below are a sample, not the picture.

title: Lead-to-won deal ratio
question: How many enquiries does it take to win one job?
caveat: Junk enquiries lost at intake are shown separately. The excl-junk figure is the fairer one.
how_to_read: Win rate is won divided by won + lost + abandoned. Open deals are not in the denominator.

footer.learns: 15.0% of closed deals are won — 25 of 167. 17 junk enquiries were cleared at intake and 367 deals are still open.
footer.does: This is the number every hiring and ad-spend decision hangs off.

title: Leads required per month to support a new hire
question: How many enquiries a month does one more salesperson need to pay for themselves?
caveat: Recent months are incomplete — deals created lately have not had time to close.
how_to_read: Leads is deals created that month. Won is how many of those have since been won, so recent months look worse than they are.

footer.learns: 185 leads arrived in July and 18 have since been won. August brought 100 leads and 3 wins so far. Only four months are held.
footer.does: Multiply target won deals by the all-time lead-to-won ratio to get the monthly lead target.

title: Conversion rate per rep at every stage
question: Where does each salesperson’s pipeline stop?
caveat: Deals are not routed to reps at random. Charlie sends larger deals to Liam. Do not read this as a ranking of ability.
how_to_read: Read the reach-quote rate and the win-from-quote rate as two separate skills.

footer.learns: Brad carries 173 deals and wins 19% of the ones that close; Liam carries 49 and wins 35%. 90 deals have no owner at all.
footer.does: Coach the weaker of the two rates, not the overall number.

title: Rep strength — qualifying vs closing
question: Is this rep losing deals before the quote, or after it?
caveat: Deals are not routed to reps at random. Charlie sends larger deals to Liam. Do not read this as a ranking of ability.
how_to_read: Qualifying is the share of closed deals that got as far as a quote. Closing is the share of those that were won.

footer.learns: Liam qualifies 71% and closes 50%. Brad qualifies only 22% but closes 85% of what he quotes. Ella closes 8%.
footer.does: Low qualifying means a front-end problem. Low closing means a pricing or objection problem.

legends.label: Qualifying — share that reached a quote
Qualifying — share that reached a quote

title: Won value by intake route
question: Which way of arriving produces the most money?
caveat: Empty opportunity.inquiry is a data-quality flag, not a lead source. Paid-click arrivals are now split from free ones: 47 paid website-form deals and 12 paid hand-created deals.
how_to_read: Route is worked out from which enquiry-text field is filled. Blank means the deal was typed in by hand.

footer.learns: £634,815 of won work came from deals typed in by hand, against £252,994 from the enquiries@ inbox. Paid clicks brought 59 deals and £14,166 of won work between them.
footer.does: The hand-created bar is usually the sales team’s own contacts. Treat it separately from marketing.

blocks.subtitle: Hand-created deals by recorded lead source
blocks.label: sortable table — stored on the 14 Sept run, not this one

title: Revenue from repeat customers and referrals
question: How much of the money comes from people who already knew us?
caveat: Lead source is blank on a large share of deals — 170 of them, carrying £527,111 of won work. Referral — Domestic and Referral — Commercial exist as options but are recorded on zero BGD deals.
how_to_read: Bars are won value against the rep-recorded Lead source field. The tail row holds eight values with a single deal each and no won work.

footer.learns: The old “other recorded source” bar was 17 separate values. Enquiries@ holds the most deals (142) for a 9% win rate, Crittall holds 92 for £25,300, and one Self Generated deal carries £95,560. Repeat Customer still wins 3 of its 4 closed deals on 12 deals.
footer.does: Repeat wins at six times the rate of the brand inbox, on a twelfth of the volume. Referral cannot be answered at all until reps start ticking it.

title: Time from enquiry to won deal, by source
question: How long does each kind of enquiry take to turn into money?
caveat: Same-day wins are usually deals entered after the fact, not fast sales. Two of the four routes have fewer than eight won deals behind them.
how_to_read: Median days from deal creation to the day it was marked won, with the shortest and longest either side.

footer.learns: Won deals take 22 to 42 days from enquiry on median depending on the route, and hand-created ones range from same-day to 94 days.
footer.does: Short cycles let you forecast. Long ones need a reason.

title: Which sources fail at which stage
question: Do different lead sources die at different points?
how_to_read: Each bar is one route, split by the stage where its deals died.

footer.learns: The enquiries@ inbox and the website form lose most of their deals before a quote goes out. Hand-created deals mostly win.
footer.does: A route that dies before qualification is a targeting problem.

title: Does replying fast increase the win rate
question: Do deals answered quickly win more often?
caveat: Phone calls are invisible here. A deal shown as never answered may have been rung.
how_to_read: Every bar must show the number of deals behind it. Some buckets are tiny.

footer.learns: 8 of the 13 deals answered within the hour were won — 62%. Of the 20 never answered in writing, none were won.
footer.does: If the within-an-hour bar is clearly higher, set a response-time rule.

title: Response time by rep
question: How fast does each person answer a customer?
caveat: Deals are not routed to reps at random. Charlie sends larger deals to Liam. Written messages only — calls are not counted.
how_to_read: Median is the typical reply. The 90th percentile is the bad days, and it is the one customers remember.

footer.learns: Liam replies in 2.1 hours on median, Chris in 54.1. But Liam’s 90th percentile is 170 hours, so the bad days are bad for everyone.
footer.does: A good median with a terrible p90 means no cover when someone is busy.

title: Open deals nobody has replied to
question: How many live enquiries have never had a written answer?
caveat: A deal counted here may have been telephoned. Check before accusing anyone.
how_to_read: Counts open deals with no outbound message to the customer, ever.

footer.learns: 131 of 367 open deals have never had a written reply, and 115 of those have been waiting more than seven days.
footer.does: This is the list to work through on Monday morning.

blocks.subtitle: The deals themselves
blocks.label: sortable table with drill — 269 rows, regenerate on demand

title: Deals gone quiet
question: Which live deals have had no activity for a month or more?
how_to_read: Idle means no message, note or stage change. The money column is quoted value sitting still.

footer.learns: 109 of the 204 open deals at Quote Sent have been idle for 30 days or more, holding £1,971,640 of quoted work.
footer.does: Anything idle past 30 days at Quote Sent needs a call this week.

title: Messages per won deal vs per lost deal
question: Do won deals involve more conversation?
caveat: Message assignment coverage is low. Most closed deals have no assigned messages at all.
how_to_read: Only deals with at least one assigned customer message are counted.

footer.learns: Won deals carry a median of 9 customer messages, lost deals 2 and abandoned 1 — on the 58 closed deals that have any messages assigned.
footer.does: If won deals average far more messages, the lost ones were never really conversations.

title: Stage deals sit in longest before being lost
question: Where do deals stall before they die?
caveat: Deals whose longest stage lasted under a day are junk clearing, not stalls.
how_to_read: The longest stage each deal sat in before closing. Duration is capped at the close date.

footer.learns: Deals that die at Waiting On Details sit there 40.8 days on median, and one in ten sits 68 days.
footer.does: A long stall at one stage usually means the customer is waiting for something from us.

title: Which buyer type gets furthest
question: Which kind of customer makes it to deposit most often, and which is a small share of enquiries but a large share of the money?
caveat: Buyer type is ticked on roughly a quarter of deals — 95 of them. This is a slice, not the whole pipeline.
how_to_read: Only deals with a buyer type ticked appear here. Both percentages in the second chart are of typed deals only.

footer.learns: Contractors are 42% of typed leads and 76% of typed won value, and win 43% of their closed deals. Architects have won none of 13.
footer.does: Aim marketing at whichever type reaches deposit most reliably. A type with a small lead share and a large revenue share is where the marketing should point.

blocks.subtitle: How far each buyer type gets
Share of leads against share of revenue

title: Product type conversion and value
question: On how many deals do we know what was being sold?
caveat: Product type is recorded on a minority of deals. Every product has fewer than eighteen deals behind it.
how_to_read: Coverage first — the second chart only covers deals with a product type recorded. Win rate is on closed deals only; products with no closed deals show blank, not zero.

footer.learns: Product type is recorded on 94 of 535 deals and on 11 of the 36 won. Cortizo casement and bi-folding doors carry the most won value, £136,499 each.
footer.does: Make product type mandatory at quote stage, and push the products that both win and carry value.

title: Open deals with no next action set
question: Which live deals have nobody scheduled to do anything?
how_to_read: No open task on the deal and none on the contact either.

footer.learns: 62 of 202 open deals at Quote Sent have no open task and 91 have one overdue — £2,017,477 with nothing scheduled.
footer.does: Every deal past Quote Sent should have a next action and a date.

title: Open deals with no notes
question: How many notes exist, and who writes them?
how_to_read: Counts notes, their typical length, and how many people write them. Thin means under 100 characters of note text in total.

footer.learns: 141 notes exist, median 158 characters, written by 6 people. But 174 of the 202 open deals at Quote Sent have no note at all.
footer.does: If one person writes all the notes, the knowledge leaves when they do.

blocks.subtitle: Open deals with no notes, by stage

title: Deals with most information missing
question: How much do we actually know about each live deal?
how_to_read: Six fields: owner, value, enquiry text, lead source, buyer type, product type. Weak means three fields or fewer.

footer.learns: 121 of 354 open deals have two of the six fields filled or fewer; 40 have all six. Records improve with stage — 1.5 at Marketing Qualified, 4.2 at Negotiation.
footer.does: Anything scoring three or less cannot be forecast. Weak records at Negotiation are the dangerous ones.

title: Mandatory fields left empty, by rep
question: Who is not filling the fields in, and who follows the process?
caveat: Deals are not routed to reps at random. Charlie sends larger deals to Liam. Do not read this as a ranking of ability.
how_to_read: Colour is the number of that rep’s open deals with the field empty. The second chart measures three habits separately — a rep can be good at one and bad at another.

footer.learns: Buyer type is empty on 116 of Brad’s open deals — £2,066,277 of open value. He sets a next action on 56% of them and writes a note on none.
footer.does: Make buyer type and product type mandatory before a quote can be sent. Then pick the one habit that matters most and fix it across the team first.

blocks.subtitle: How often each rep follows the process

title: Phrases customers use for what they want
question: On how many closed deals do we have the original enquiry text?
caveat: Keyword matching on enquiry text. A phrase can appear on a deal about something else.
how_to_read: Usable means 60 characters or more of enquiry text. Phrase is the customer’s word; our term is the business’s name for it.

footer.learns: Of 181 closed deals, 123 carry enquiry text and 116 are usable. 19 enquiries use the word “replace” and 18 say “crittall”.
footer.does: Empty enquiry text is a data-quality flag. Use their words in ad copy and page headings, not ours.
